templates.name: Main purpose: literary reaction, mood or trait
Function: example or supporting detail for a claim
Main purpose: profile of a person, work or institution
Three moves: explains a finding, generalizes it to a pattern, explains an exception
Three moves: introduces a phenomenon, rules out two explanations, presents a plausible third
Function: set-up or context for what follows
Describes a problem in research on a topic, then sketches a researcher’s approach to it

items.passage: Phoenician ceramic flasks circulated through a regional commercial network in the southern Levant during the early Iron Age, roughly the eleventh to the mid-ninth century BCE. Using gas chromatography to analyze organic residues absorbed into the walls of 27 such flasks from five archaeological sites in Israel, Dvory Namdar and colleagues detected cinnamaldehyde, a principal component of cinnamon, in 10 of them. Because the cinnamon tree grew exclusively in South and Southeast Asia in antiquity, the researchers propose that, provided the compound derived from cinnamon bark, the flasks may indicate long-distance trade with that region.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It explains how researchers determined that Phoenician flasks recovered at sites in Israel had originally been manufactured in South and Southeast Asia.
It describes an analysis of residues preserved in ancient flasks and explains why the results led researchers to revise the dates previously assigned to the flasks.
It presents a chemical study of ancient containers whose results, if correctly interpreted, suggest a trade connection that spanned a great distance.
It summarizes research on early Iron Age flasks that identified the main routes by which Phoenician goods spread across the southern Levant.
items.explanation: The text describes how Namdar and colleagues analyzed “organic residues absorbed into the walls of 27 such flasks” and detected cinnamaldehyde, “a principal component of cinnamon,” in 10 of them. It then notes that “the cinnamon tree grew exclusively in South and Southeast Asia in antiquity,” so the researchers propose that, “provided the compound derived from cinnamon bark, the flasks may indicate long-distance trade with that region.” The text therefore presents a chemical study whose results, if correctly interpreted, suggest a trade connection across a great distance, as choice C says.

A.recipe: SWAP: right study, the far-off origin moved from the cinnamon to the flasks
A.why_wrong: The text says the cinnamon tree grew in South and Southeast Asia; it says nothing about where the flasks themselves were made and calls them “Phoenician ceramic flasks.”

B.recipe: INV: first part true, invented result (redating)
B.why_wrong: The text does describe a residue analysis, but the dates it gives for the flasks are background; nothing suggests the study changed them.

D.recipe: INV: first part true, invented finding built on the word “network”
D.why_wrong: The text mentions that the flasks circulated through “a regional commercial network,” but the study identified a substance inside them, not the routes by which goods moved.

sources.what: Namdar, Gilboa, Neumann, Finkelstein, Weiner 2013, Mediterranean Archaeology and Archaeometry 13(2): lipid residues in 27 early Iron Age (11th to mid-9th c. BCE) Phoenician flasks from five sites in Israel analyzed by GC-MS; 10 contained cinnamaldehyde; the cinnamon tree grew only in South and Southeast Asia in antiquity, so long-distance trade is possible if the compound came from cinnamon bark

items.notes: Area: history and archaeological science. Key C. Band 6 (P_study has a band-7 item, but the plan sets this cell to 6). Key parts: 2 (a chemical study of containers; a possible long-distance trade link, hedged as the passage hedges). Distractors: A and D keep a true first part (researchers studied the flasks; research on the flasks) and fail later; B keeps the analysis and invents a redating. Key paraphrases away from the passage (containers, a great distance). Passage keeps the source’s caution (“provided the compound did come from cinnamon bark”).

band7.why: Template has band-7 official items (82cb7dda), but the plan sets 6. Hedged two-part key paraphrased away from the passage; A, B and D keep a true first part (the researchers studied the flasks) and each fails on one later claim (flask origin, redating, routes), the band-6 profile.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from George Crabbe’s 1783 poem “The Village.” Earlier in the poem, the speaker observes that poets have long portrayed the lives of country people as carefree.

I grant indeed that fields and flocks have charms
For him that grazes or for him that farms;
But, when amid such pleasing scenes I trace
The poor laborious natives of the place,
And see the mid-day sun, with fervid ray,
On their bare heads and dewy temples play;
While some, with feebler heads and fainter hearts,
Deplore their fortune, yet sustain their parts:
Then shall I dare these real ills to hide
In tinsel trappings of poetic pride?
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To convey the speaker’s reluctance to conceal the hardships of rural laborers behind ornamental poetic language
To praise rural laborers for enduring their difficult lives without ever expressing discontent about them
To argue that the countryside offers pleasures to visitors that the people who farm the land are unable to appreciate
To express the speaker’s regret that he lacks the skill to describe rural scenes as vividly as other poets have done
items.explanation: The speaker grants that “fields and flocks have charms,” but when he sees “the poor laborious natives of the place” working under “the mid-day sun,” some of whom “deplore their fortune,” he asks, “Then shall I dare these real ills to hide / In tinsel trappings of poetic pride?” The question implies that he will not hide these “real ills” behind showy, flattering verse. The text therefore conveys the speaker’s reluctance to conceal rural laborers’ hardships behind ornamental poetic language.

B.recipe: PART plus REV: true that some laborers endure, false that none complain
B.why_wrong: Some laborers “sustain their parts,” but the same line says they “deplore their fortune,” so they do express discontent; and the speaker’s point concerns how poets should portray them, not praise for their silence.

C.recipe: STANCE plus INV: an argument and a visitor-versus-farmer contrast the text never makes
C.why_wrong: The speaker grants that the countryside has charms “for him that grazes or for him that farms,” that is, for the people who work it; he never claims they cannot appreciate those charms.

D.recipe: LIT: “tinsel trappings of poetic pride” literalized into a lack of skill
D.why_wrong: The speaker does not doubt his own skill; he questions whether he should decorate “real ills” with “tinsel trappings,” which other poets use and he rejects.

sources.what: George Crabbe, The Village (1783), Book I, lines 39 to 48, text as printed in George Crabbe: Poems, Volume 1, ed. Adolphus William Ward (Cambridge, 1905); the editor’s variants list gives “gazes” for “grazes” in line 40 of the 1783 first edition, the only change in these lines, hence “adapted”

items.notes: Area: literature (poem, 1783). Key A. Band 6 (hard P_lit band-6 models 3.15 and 3.19 are poems; band-7 model 3.3). Crabbe appears nowhere in the bank or in any official item. Context line is accurate: lines 7 to 38 of Book I criticize pastoral poets who sing “of happy swains, / Because the Muses never knew their pains.” Distractors: B partly right (endurance) and wrong on “never expressing discontent”; C an argument built on the farm line; D literalizes the closing image. Key verb convey; key not the longest option.

band7.why: Pre-1800 verse whose closing rhetorical question must be read as a refusal; B is half right (the laborers endure) and fails on “never expressing discontent”, C misreads the farm line, D literalizes the closing image. Each wrong option falls to one careful reread, as in the band-6 P_lit poems 3.15 and 3.19.

items.passage: Economic historian Jan de Vries has argued that early modern Europe experienced an “industrious revolution”: between about 1600 and 1800, households gave up leisure and redirected their labor toward paid work, spending the proceeds on manufactured goods they had once produced at home. De Vries treats this change and the subsequent Industrial Revolution as parts of a single continuum. Akira Hayami, who coined the term, rejects that interpretation. <u>Hayami had introduced the phrase in 1967 to characterize Tokugawa Japan (1603–1868), where scarce capital produced an economy that absorbed ever more labor, in contrast to Britain’s capital-intensive industrialization.</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It gives an example of the shift from producing goods at home to earning wages that de Vries describes earlier in the text.
It presents a case that de Vries cites in support of his view that industrious and industrial revolutions form a continuum.
It explains why Hayami concluded that Tokugawa Japan never went on to develop an industrial economy.
It clarifies the reasoning behind the objection that the originator of a term raises to another historian’s use of it.
items.explanation: The text says that de Vries treats the industrious revolution and the Industrial Revolution “as parts of a single continuum” and that Hayami, “who coined the term, rejects that interpretation.” The underlined sentence explains why: Hayami used the phrase for a Japanese economy that “absorbed ever more labor, in contrast to Britain’s capital-intensive industrialization,” so for him the two are opposites, not stages of one process. The sentence thus clarifies the reasoning behind Hayami’s objection.

A.recipe: SWAP: a true theme (more labor) assigned to the wrong place and argument
A.why_wrong: The underlined sentence concerns Tokugawa Japan and Hayami’s use of the term, not the European households that de Vries describes, and it offers no example of people giving up home production.

B.recipe: STANCE: right case, wrong holder and reversed role
B.why_wrong: The case of Tokugawa Japan belongs to Hayami, and it is presented as the basis for rejecting the continuum de Vries proposes, not as support for it.

C.recipe: INV: a conclusion about Japan’s later history the text never mentions
C.why_wrong: The text contrasts Japan’s labor-absorbing economy with Britain’s industrialization in the period Hayami studied; it says nothing about whether Japan later industrialized.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Industrious Revolution: term coined by Akira Hayami in a 1967 work to contrast labor-intensive Tokugawa Japan (1603 to 1868), whose path absorbed increasing labor because capital was scarce, with the capital-intensive British Industrial Revolution; Jan de Vries’s version for early modern Europe (about 1600 to 1800): households shift labor to market work, reduce leisure and buy commercially produced goods; Hayami objects that de Vries treats the industrious and industrial revolutions as a continuum, while he sees them as opposing concepts

items.notes: Area: social science (economic history). Key D. Band 6; modelled on 9b01bcf4 (3.10, “helps explain Cruse’s position”) and 2e744883 (3.12). Key parts: 2 (clarifies reasoning; behind an objection to another historian’s use of a term). Distractors: A and B start from a true idea (labor shifts; de Vries’s continuum) and fail on whose case it is; C invents a later history. The deciding sentence (“rejects that view”) precedes the span, and the span itself must be read as the reason for it.

band7.why: The span is a means (the reason behind Hayami’s objection) and the key is abstract and two-part; A and B start from true ideas in the text (de Vries’s labor shift, his continuum) and fail on whose case it is. Near the section 5 F_example recipe, but each wrong option still falls to one stated fact; plan target 6 met.

items.passage: Hortus Malabaricus, a twelve-volume botanical survey describing more than 700 plants of the Malabar Coast in present-day Kerala, India, began appearing in Amsterdam in 1678. It bears the name of its compiler, Hendrik van Rheede, the Dutch colonial administrator of Malabar, but its contents depend substantially on indigenous expertise: Itty Achudan, a traditional physician from Kerala’s Ezhava community, selected the specimens to be illustrated and dictated their descriptions and medicinal applications in Malayalam, and three Konkani Brahmin physicians subsequently verified the material. The volumes record each plant’s name in Malayalam, Konkani, and Arabic in addition to Latin.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain how a colonial governor’s botanical research changed the way plants were named in European scientific works
To describe a seventeenth-century botanical work and show the large part local practitioners played in producing it
To compare the plant knowledge of healers in Kerala with that of the European scholars who later published it
To argue that a celebrated botanical work owes far less to its Dutch compiler than historians have generally recognized
items.explanation: The text first describes Hortus Malabaricus, “a twelve-volume botanical survey describing more than 700 plants of the Malabar Coast.” It then explains that although the work “bears the name of its compiler,” its “contents depend substantially on indigenous expertise”: Itty Achudan selected the specimens and dictated their descriptions, and “three Konkani Brahmin physicians subsequently verified the material.” The text therefore describes a seventeenth-century botanical work and shows the large part local practitioners played in producing it.

A.recipe: INV plus BROAD: an influence on European naming the text never claims
A.why_wrong: The text says the volumes record plant names in several languages, but it never says the work changed how plants were named in European science, and it credits the contents to local experts rather than to van Rheede’s own research.

C.recipe: INV: a comparison of two bodies of knowledge that the text does not make
C.why_wrong: The text says what the local experts contributed; it never describes any separate knowledge held by European scholars, so there is no comparison.

D.recipe: STANCE plus INV: the key’s point recast as an argument against historians
D.why_wrong: The text does say the contents “depend substantially on indigenous expertise,” but it reports this neutrally; it never calls the work celebrated or claims that historians have failed to recognize the experts’ role.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Hortus Malabaricus: 12 volumes compiled by Hendrik van Rheede, governor of Dutch Malabar, published in Amsterdam from 1678; more than 742 plants, 794 copperplate engravings; Itty Achudan, an Ezhava physician, disclosed the knowledge, his team selected the plants to be drawn, and he dictated the material in Malayalam, which was translated into Latin; the material was scrutinized by three Konkani Brahmins (Ranga Bhat, Vinayaka Pandit, Appu Bhat); plant names recorded in Malayalam, Konkani and Arabic besides Latin

items.notes: Area: history of science. Key B. Band 6 (P_profile has no band-7 official item). The end date is left out because the source gives both 1693 and 1703. Key parts: 2 (describe the work; explain its dependence on local experts). Distractors: D is the near miss (agrees that the contents rest on local experts but turns a neutral profile into an argument about historians); A and C invent an influence and a comparison. Compare is never keyed in the official bank, as here.

fixes: key paraphrased away from the passage (“explain how much it depended on the knowledge of local experts” echoed “depend substantially on indigenous expertise”); now “show the large part local practitioners played in producing it”, and no longer the longest option

band7.why: P_profile has no band-7 official items (band7 file section 5), so a strong band 6 is the ceiling. Key now paraphrased away from the passage; D is the near miss (agrees on the local experts, adds an argument against historians the text never makes).

items.passage: Little brown bats infected with the fungus responsible for white-nose syndrome die in great numbers during hibernation, and DeeAnn Reeder and colleagues found evidence suggesting why: infected bats arouse from hibernation more frequently than uninfected bats, and each arousal to a warm body temperature depletes fat reserves the animals need to survive the winter. Indiana, northern, and tricolored bats have likewise suffered severe winter mortality from the disease. The big brown bat (Eptesicus fuscus) is an exception: it is highly resistant to infection, which researchers have linked partly to fatty acids in its wing skin that inhibit the fungus’s growth.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It reports and explains a finding about a disease’s effect on one species, notes that other species are similarly affected, and then presents a resistant species and a possible reason for its resistance.

It presents a study showing how and why a disease harms one bat species, indicates that other species have suffered in the same way, and then describes an exception that undermines the study’s explanation.

It describes and accounts for the harm a disease causes one species, extends that observation to several related species, and then predicts that those species will gradually acquire resistance to the disease.
It reports a finding about a disease’s effect on one species, attributes that finding to a flaw in the way the study was designed, and then describes a species that resists the disease.
items.explanation: The text first reports that infected little brown bats “die in great numbers during hibernation” and explains why, citing Reeder and colleagues’ evidence: infected bats “arouse from hibernation more frequently than uninfected bats,” and each arousal “depletes fat reserves the animals need to survive the winter.” It then notes that “Indiana, northern, and tricolored bats have likewise suffered severe winter mortality.” Finally, it presents the big brown bat as “an exception” that “is highly resistant to infection” and gives a possible reason, fatty acids “that inhibit the fungus’s growth.” Choice A describes this structure.

B.recipe: moves 1 and 2 right, move 3 a stance flip (exception undermines the explanation)
B.why_wrong: The big brown bat’s resistance to infection does not challenge the explanation that frequent arousals deplete infected bats’ fat; the text simply presents the species as an exception and links its resistance to fatty acids in its skin.

C.recipe: moves 1 and 2 right, move 3 an invented prediction
C.why_wrong: The text never predicts that the affected species will develop resistance; the only resistant species it mentions is the big brown bat, which it presents as an exception.

D.why_wrong: The text presents Reeder and colleagues’ evidence as reliable and uses it to explain the bats’ deaths; it never suggests that the research was flawed.

sources.what: Reeder et al. 2012, PLoS ONE 7(6): e38920: dataloggers on 504 little brown bats; WNS-affected bats aroused to euthermic temperatures more frequently than unaffected bats, likely contributing to mortality; arousals are normal but deplete fat stores

Ingala, Ravenelle, Monro, Frank 2017, PLoS ONE 12(10): e0187195: WNS greatly increases over-winter mortality of little brown, Indiana, northern and tricolored bats; big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus) are highly resistant to Pd infections; wing-epidermis fatty acids (four of which, and 1-oleoglycerol found in E. fuscus, inhibit Pd growth)

items.notes: Area: natural science (wildlife disease). Key A. band_target 6, not the plan’s 7: spec/rw/band7/text_structure_and_purpose.md lists no band-7 official item for S16 (its only official item, 4ed09415 / 3.17, is band 6), and WAVE.md says such cells are written as strong band 6 (make_plan.py alternated 7/6 because this skill’s band-7 file has no appendix table). Three moves; B and C keep moves 1 and 2 (in different words, to avoid a shared option prefix) and break move 3 (stance flip, invented prediction), D breaks move 2, as in 3.17’s distractors. The finding is the little brown bats’ mortality in hibernation and its account is Reeder’s arousal evidence (Reeder leaves open why infected bats arouse more, so the passage does not explain that); the pattern sentence rests on the mortality the Ingala abstract reports for the other species, and the exception is hedged (“linked partly”). Key wording avoids 3.17’s key (“describes and accounts for a finding ... characterizes the finding as representative of a general pattern”).

band7.why: S16 has no band-7 official items (its only official item, 4ed09415, is band 6), so band 6 is the ceiling. B and C keep moves 1 and 2 and fail on move 3 (a stance flip, an invented prediction), D fails on move 2, as in 4ed09415.

items.passage: From about 1980, tracking data from the Pioneer 10 and 11 spacecraft revealed a puzzling discrepancy: as both probes traveled outward, they were slowing slightly more than predicted, as if subject to a faint, constant sunward acceleration. Drag from interplanetary gas and dust was considered, but the measured density of that material is too low to produce it. An unrecognized gravitational influence fares no better, since the orbits of the outer planets show no corresponding deviation. Slava Turyshev and colleagues’ 2012 reanalysis offers the most compelling account: heat radiated unevenly from the spacecraft generated a recoil force matching the anomaly.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It presents a puzzling measurement, explains why two proposed causes of it are untenable, and then attributes the measurement to errors in the way the spacecraft were tracked.
It describes an unexpected observation, discusses two explanations for it that the author finds unconvincing, and then states that a satisfactory account of it has yet to emerge.
It reports an astronomical finding, presents two competing accounts of it that the author considers equally plausible, and then describes a study that combined those accounts.
It introduces an unexplained effect on the motion of two spacecraft, explains why two candidate causes can be dismissed, and then endorses a later study’s explanation.
items.explanation: The text opens with an anomaly: the Pioneer probes “were slowing slightly more than predicted.” It then dismisses two candidate causes, drag, because “the measured density of that material is too low to produce it,” and an unrecognized gravitational influence, because “the orbits of the outer planets show no corresponding deviation.” Finally, it calls Turyshev and colleagues’ 2012 reanalysis “the most compelling account,” endorsing their explanation that unevenly radiated heat “generated a recoil force matching the anomaly.” Choice D describes this structure.

A.recipe: moves 1 and 2 right, move 3 invented (tracking errors)
A.why_wrong: The text never says the anomaly came from tracking errors; the account it favors is a real physical force, “a recoil force” produced by unevenly radiated heat.

B.recipe: moves 1 and 2 right, move 3 reversed (no account yet)
B.why_wrong: The author does not say that a convincing account is still missing; the text calls Turyshev and colleagues’ 2012 reanalysis “the most compelling account.”

C.recipe: move 2 stance flip (equally plausible) and move 3 invented
C.why_wrong: The author rejects both drag and an unrecognized gravitational influence rather than considering them plausible, and the favored study does not combine them; it attributes the anomaly to heat.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Pioneer anomaly: first noticed around 1980; approximately constant sunward acceleration; drag rejected because measured densities are too small; gravitational explanations rejected because the acceleration does not appear in the orbits of the outer planets; resolved as thermal recoil

Turyshev, Toth, Kinsella, Lee, Lok, Ellis 2012, Physical Review Letters 108, 241101 (arXiv 1204.2507), Support for the thermal origin of the Pioneer anomaly: thermal recoil force from anisotropic emission of heat; once accounted for, no anomalous acceleration remains

items.notes: Area: natural science (astrophysics, spacecraft navigation). Key D. Band 7, modelled on 6ae393f7 (3.11). Band-7 moves: three moves stated abstractly with move 3 carrying the author’s stance (“most compelling”); A and B keep moves 1 and 2 and fail only in move 3 (an invented cause; a reversed stance), C fails from move 2. Key avoids 3.11’s wording (refutes, plausible) and its signal phrases (not attributable to, Instead, likely correct). Key 26 words after review (shortened so it is not the longest option); options 26 to 29 words.
band7_moves: three moves stated abstractly, move 3 carrying the author’s stance (endorses the 2012 account as “most compelling”)
two distractors (A, B) right in moves 1 and 2 and wrong only in move 3 (invented tracking errors; reversed stance, no account yet)
abstract key with almost no passage wording (anomaly, candidate causes, a more recent study’s account)

fixes: B no longer copies 6ae393f7’s option wording (“that the author regards as flawed”, “has yet to”): now “finds unconvincing”, “a satisfactory account”
key no longer echoes the passage’s “anomaly” and “account” and is no longer the longest option (26 words)

band7.why: Tracks 6ae393f7: three moves stated abstractly, move 3 carrying the author’s stance (“most compelling”); A and B keep moves 1 and 2 and fail only on move 3 (a misplaced cause, a reversed stance), C fails from move 2; key no longer echoes the passage. The Pioneer anomaly is popular science, but the passage supplies its own resolution, so background knowledge buys nothing on a structure stem.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Edmund Gosse’s 1907 memoir Father and Son, in which Gosse recalls an incident from his early childhood.

I confused [my father] in some sense with God; at all events I believed that my Father knew everything and saw everything. One morning in my sixth year, my Mother and I were alone in the morning-room, when my Father came in and announced some fact to us. The shock to me was as that of a thunderbolt, for what my Father had said “was not true.” My Mother gently told him so, and he accepted the correction. Nothing could possibly have been more trifling to my parents, but to me it meant an epoch.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe how the narrator’s mother taught him to question the things his father told him
To recount how a seemingly trivial event overturned a young child’s belief that his father knew everything
To show that the narrator’s parents frequently disagreed about what had actually happened
To convey the narrator’s fear that he would be punished for pointing out his father’s error
items.explanation: The narrator says that as a child he “believed that my Father knew everything and saw everything.” He then describes a morning when his father announced something that “was not true,” and his mother corrected him. Although “nothing could possibly have been more trifling to my parents,” for the narrator “it meant an epoch.” The text therefore recounts how a seemingly trivial event overturned the child’s belief that his father knew everything.

A.recipe: SWAP plus INV: the mother’s one correction turned into a lesson for the child
A.why_wrong: The mother corrects the father, not the child, and she does so “gently” on one occasion; the text never says she taught the narrator to question his father.

C.recipe: BROAD: one mild correction stretched into frequent disagreement
C.why_wrong: The text describes a single “trifling” correction that the father “accepted”; it never says the parents often disagreed.

D.recipe: INV: a fear of punishment the text never mentions
D.why_wrong: The narrator does not point out the error; his mother does. His shock comes from discovering that his father could be wrong, not from fear of being punished.

sources.what: Edmund Gosse, Father and Son (1907), chapter II, the incident in his sixth year; text copied from Project Gutenberg #2540, trimmed at sentence boundaries (the sentence about the narrator standing on the rug and looking into the fire, and the one about mother and son knowing the facts, left out), “[my father]” replaces “him”, single quotes made double with the period moved inside

items.notes: Area: literature (memoir, 1907). Key B. Medium P_lit; the key is the longest option here (one of the batch’s planned key-longest items). Gosse appears nowhere in the bank or the official items. Distractors: A SWAP (who corrects whom), C BROAD, D INV. Key paraphrases “trifling” and “epoch” (seemingly trivial event; overturned a belief).

fixes: period moved inside the closing quotation mark (“was not true.”), CB style
source note now names the two sentences actually left out (the rug and fire sentence; mother and son knowing the facts)

items.passage: In his 1935 book Genesis and Development of a Scientific Fact, Polish microbiologist Ludwik Fleck argued that scientific knowledge is produced collectively, within communities of researchers whose shared assumptions shape what they observe; he called such communities “thought collectives.” <u>Fleck’s central case was the history of the Wassermann reaction, a diagnostic blood test for syphilis.</u> Although August von Wassermann later remembered the test’s development as a direct path toward a goal he had planned from the start, Fleck maintained that it had actually emerged through a meandering, collective process marked by exchanges and misunderstandings.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It introduces a medical test that, according to Fleck, Wassermann developed without help from other researchers.
It explains why the communities of researchers described in the previous sentence seldom agreed about the value of the test.
It identifies the main example that Fleck used to illustrate the view described in the previous sentence.
It describes a discovery that Fleck credited with first leading him to study how scientific knowledge is produced.
items.explanation: The first sentence presents Fleck’s argument that “scientific knowledge is produced collectively, within communities of researchers,” which he called “thought collectives.” The underlined sentence names “Fleck’s central case,” the history of the Wassermann reaction, and the last sentence shows how that history fits his argument: Wassermann “later remembered the test’s development as a direct path,” but Fleck maintained that it “had actually emerged through a meandering, collective process.” The underlined sentence therefore identifies the main example that Fleck used to illustrate the view described in the previous sentence.

A.recipe: REV: the collective process Fleck describes turned into a lone achievement
A.why_wrong: Fleck maintained that the test “had actually emerged through a meandering, collective process”; it was Wassermann’s later memory, not Fleck, that presented the work as “a direct path toward a goal he had planned from the start.”

B.recipe: INV: a disagreement about the test’s value the text never mentions
B.why_wrong: The text mentions “exchanges and misunderstandings” during the test’s development, but it never says researchers disagreed about the test’s value, and the underlined sentence explains nothing about the communities in the previous sentence.

D.recipe: INV: a causal origin the text never claims
D.why_wrong: The text calls the Wassermann reaction “Fleck’s central case,” the example he used to support his argument; it never says the test first led him to study how scientific knowledge is produced.

sources.what: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Ludwik Fleck: Genesis and Development of a Scientific Fact (1935); cognition is a collective activity and facts emerge within thought collectives shaped by thought styles; syphilis research and the Wassermann reaction are his central case; success is achievable only if the whole group of scholars is engaged; after fifteen years an identification between results and intentions had taken place in Wassermann’s thinking, so the meandering process of development came to look a straight, goal-directed path

items.notes: Area: humanities and science (history and philosophy of science). Key C. Medium F_example modelled on 2.12 (claim, then the example the underlined span introduces) and 2.1. Reviewer replacement for the Shklovsky and Kholstomer item, a round-1 subject (round-1 TSP item 18, same frame and distractors) already swapped out of a live item once. The test’s date is left out because the fetched page does not give it. Distractors: A REV (a lone achievement against the collective process), B INV, D INV (a causal origin). Passage kept dense on purpose: the medium tier sits at check_rw’s chars-per-word floor.

fixes: replaced: Shklovsky and Kholstomer is a round-1 subject (round-1 TSP item 18, same frame and distractors) already swapped out of a live item; new subject Ludwik Fleck’s thought collectives and the Wassermann reaction (SEP), claimed in claims.txt, key letter C kept, passage dense on purpose to hold the medium chars-per-word floor

items.passage: Vincent van Gogh frequently painted over his earlier work, and roughly 30 percent of his paintings are thought to conceal other compositions. Conventional imaging methods had detected only the vague outline of a head beneath his Patch of Grass (1887), too indistinct to reveal any facial features. <u>To obtain a clearer view, Joris Dik and colleagues scanned a section of the canvas with an intense synchrotron X-ray beam, which caused the chemical elements in the concealed paint layer to emit characteristic radiation.</u> Maps of mercury, from the red pigment vermilion, and of antimony were then combined into a color image of a woman’s face.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It describes the technique researchers used to reveal an image hidden beneath a painting’s surface.
It explains why van Gogh frequently painted over his earlier work rather than starting each new painting on a fresh canvas.
It identifies the pigments van Gogh used when he painted the landscape visible in Patch of Grass.
It presents evidence that challenges an earlier claim about who painted the concealed portrait.
items.explanation: The text explains that conventional imaging methods detected only “the vague outline of a head” beneath Patch of Grass. The underlined sentence then tells how Dik and colleagues “scanned a section of the canvas with an intense synchrotron X-ray beam,” which made the elements in “the concealed paint layer” emit radiation, and the last sentence reports the result, “a color image of a woman’s face.” The underlined sentence thus describes the technique researchers used to reveal an image hidden beneath a painting’s surface.

B.recipe: PART: restates the first sentence’s topic and adds an invented reason
B.why_wrong: The first sentence says van Gogh often painted over earlier work, but no sentence explains why, and the underlined sentence concerns the researchers’ scan.

C.recipe: SWAP: the hidden layer’s elements given to the visible landscape
C.why_wrong: The scan detected elements in “the concealed paint layer,” the portrait beneath the landscape; the text says nothing about the pigments in the visible grass painting.

D.recipe: STANCE plus INV: a dispute about authorship the text never mentions
D.why_wrong: The text raises no question about who painted the hidden portrait; it is presented as van Gogh’s own earlier work beneath the landscape.

sources.what: DESY photon science news (July 2008): Patch of Grass (Paris, 1887, Kröller-Müller Museum) conceals a woman’s head; earlier research found a vague outline of a head; Joris Dik (TU Delft) and Koen Janssens (Antwerp) used synchrotron radiation X-ray fluorescence at DORIS III, mapping mercury (vermilion) and antimony into a colour image; about thirty percent of van Gogh’s paintings conceal other compositions; published in Analytical Chemistry

Dik, Janssens et al. 2008, Analytical Chemistry 80(16): 6436-6442, abstract (Europe PMC, PMID 18662021): current museum-based imaging tools cannot properly visualize many hidden images; first use of synchrotron radiation based X-ray fluorescence mapping to visualize a woman’s head under Patch of Grass; Hg and Sb distributions gave an approximate color reconstruction

items.notes: Area: humanities and science (art conservation, X-ray imaging). Key A. Medium F_method modelled on 2.20 (the underlined sentence describes an approach researchers used) and 2.15. Distractors: B PART (first sentence), C SWAP (visible versus buried layer), D STANCE. Concept checked against the bank: no item on a hidden painting under another (pentimento and painted-over hits are different subjects).

fixes: “Conventional X-ray radiography had detected” softened to “Conventional imaging methods had detected” (DESY says only “previous research”; the paper’s abstract says museum-based imaging tools); paper abstract added as a second source

items.passage: In 1903, ceramic artist Mary Chase Perry Stratton and her business partner, Horace Caulkins, founded Pewabic Pottery in Detroit, Michigan. Caulkins, a specialist in high-temperature kilns, designed the Revelation kiln, and the studio soon became known for its shimmering, iridescent glazes. Those glazes can still be seen on tiles in buildings such as the Detroit Public Library and the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception in Washington, DC. Designated a National Historic Landmark in 1991, Pewabic continues to operate today as a nonprofit educational institution that offers ceramics classes, holds exhibitions, and sells pottery made on site.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall purpose of the text?
options: To explain how Pewabic Pottery’s glazes changed the design of public buildings across the United States
To compare the contributions that Pewabic Pottery’s two founders made to the studio’s early success
To describe the methods Pewabic Pottery uses today to teach ceramics to students
To trace the history of a ceramics studio from its founding to the present day
items.explanation: The text begins with Pewabic Pottery’s founding “in 1903,” describes the studio’s kiln and “iridescent glazes,” names buildings where its tiles “can still be seen,” and ends by noting that Pewabic “continues to operate today as a nonprofit educational institution.” The text therefore traces the history of the studio from its founding to the present day.

A.recipe: BROAD: two buildings stretched to public architecture across the country
A.why_wrong: The text names two buildings with Pewabic tiles; it never says the glazes changed the design of public buildings nationwide.

B.recipe: INV: a comparison the text does not make
B.why_wrong: The text mentions what each founder did, but only in passing, and it never weighs their contributions against each other.

C.why_wrong: The text says only that Pewabic offers ceramics classes; it never describes how they are taught, and the classes are just one part of the studio’s history.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Pewabic Pottery: founded 1903 in Detroit by Mary Chase Perry Stratton with business partner Horace James Caulkins, a high-heat and kiln specialist who developed the Revelation kiln; known for iridescent glazes; tile in the Detroit Public Library and the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception; National Historic Landmark 1991; operates as a non-profit educational institution with classes, exhibitions and pottery sales

items.notes: Area: humanities (ceramics, decorative arts). Key D. Medium P_profile modelled on 2.5 (overview of an institution’s founding and later life). Stem is 2.5’s “overall purpose” variant. Key does not list the passage’s parts. Distractors: A BROAD, B INV (compare, never keyed in the bank), C PART.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from D. H. Lawrence’s 1911 novel The White Peacock, which opens with the narrator standing beside a pond near an old mill.

I stood watching the shadowy fish slide through the gloom of the mill-pond. <u>The whole place was gathered in the musing of old age.</u> The thick-piled trees on the far shore were too dark and sober to dally with the sun; the weeds stood crowded and motionless. Not even a little wind flickered the willows of the islets. The water lay softly, intensely still. Only the thin stream falling through the mill-race murmured to itself of the tumult of life which had once quickened the valley.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It elaborates on the previous sentence’s description of the fish in the pond.
It introduces an impression of the setting that the details in the following sentences develop.
It explains why the narrator has come to the mill-pond on this particular day.
It contrasts the stillness of the pond with the activity in the valley described later in the text.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence says that the whole place seemed lost in “the musing of old age,” an impression of quiet and age. The sentences that follow develop it: the trees are “too dark and sober to dally with the sun,” the weeds are “motionless,” “not even a little wind” stirs the willows, and the water lies “intensely still.” The underlined sentence therefore introduces an impression of the setting that the following details develop.

A.recipe: REL: wrong pointer (previous sentence) and wrong subject (the fish)
A.why_wrong: The underlined sentence describes “the whole place,” not the fish, and the details that bear it out come in the sentences after it.

C.recipe: INV: a purpose for the narrator’s visit the text never gives
C.why_wrong: The text never says why the narrator is at the pond; it only describes what he sees there.

D.recipe: PART plus REV: the past “tumult of life” misread as present activity
D.why_wrong: The last sentence mentions the “tumult of life which had once quickened the valley,” activity in the past; the text describes no present activity to contrast with the pond, and the underlined sentence makes no comparison.

sources.what: D. H. Lawrence, The White Peacock (1911), Part I, chapter I, opening paragraph; text copied from Project Gutenberg #38561, one sentence left out (the fish as descendants of those that darted from the monks), hence “adapted”

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1911). Key B. Medium F_setup modelled on 2.13 (Melville: the underlined sentence sets up the description that follows). Literary chosen to keep the medium tier’s literary share near CB’s (2.13 is literary). The second sentence of the original (the fish as descendants) is cut so the previous-sentence pointer in A is plainly wrong. Distractors: A REL, C INV, D PART plus REV (compare and contrast are never keyed).

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Dorothy Richardson’s 1915 novel Pointed Roofs, whose central character, Miriam, has recently finished school and is about to leave her family’s home to teach at a school in Germany.

That summer, which still seemed near to her, was going to fade and desert her, leaving nothing behind. <u>To-morrow it would belong to a world which would go on without her, taking no heed.</u> There would still be blissful days. But she would not be in them.

There would be no more silent sunny mornings with all the day ahead and nothing to do and no end anywhere to anything.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It reveals Miriam’s relief that she will soon escape the familiar routines of her family’s crowded household.
It suggests that Miriam expects the coming summer to be less pleasant than the one just past.
It conveys Miriam’s sense that the life she has enjoyed will carry on without her once she leaves.
It indicates that Miriam has already begun to forget what happened during the previous summer.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence says that the summer Miriam loved “would belong to a world which would go on without her, taking no heed.” The sentences around it reinforce this feeling: “There would still be blissful days. But she would not be in them,” and there would be “no more silent sunny mornings” for her. The sentence thus conveys Miriam’s sense that the life she has enjoyed will carry on without her once she leaves.

A.recipe: REV: sorrow at leaving read as relief
A.why_wrong: The text dwells on what Miriam will lose, such as “silent sunny mornings,” and shows no relief at going away.

B.recipe: LIT plus REV: the summer read literally and its quality reversed
B.why_wrong: The text says “there would still be blissful days”; the loss is that Miriam will not be there to enjoy them, not that they will be less pleasant.

D.recipe: REV: the summer “still seemed near to her”
D.why_wrong: The text says the summer “still seemed near to her”; Miriam fears it will fade once she leaves, not that she has already forgotten it.

sources.what: Dorothy Richardson, Pointed Roofs (1915), chapter I, section 1, Miriam’s last evening at home before leaving to teach in Germany; text copied from Project Gutenberg #3019, ending at the first clause of the next sentence (its semicolon made a period), hence “adapted”

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1915, public domain in the US). Key C. Medium F_lit modelled on 2.23 (Woolf: what a figurative span emphasizes about a character’s state). Richardson appears nowhere in the bank or the official items. Distractors: A REV (the relief Miriam feels later in the chapter is outside the excerpt), B LIT plus REV, D REV.

items.passage: Estimating how much sea level has risen since the nineteenth century requires long-term measurements, but such records are scarce in the Southern Hemisphere. John Hunter and colleagues addressed this shortage by turning to an unusual historical source at Port Arthur, Tasmania, where in 1841 Thomas Lempriere and the explorer James Clark Ross carved a sea-level benchmark into a rock face on the small Isle of the Dead. Comparing Lempriere’s tide measurements from 1841 and 1842, referenced to that benchmark, with observations made between 1999 and 2002, the researchers estimated that local sea level had risen by approximately 0.8 millimeters per year since 1841.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It explains why sea level has risen faster in the Southern Hemisphere than elsewhere, then describes a study that confirmed this pattern.
It describes a set of historical tide measurements, then explains why researchers concluded that the measurements were too unreliable to use.
It summarizes a dispute among researchers about the rate of sea-level rise, then presents evidence supporting one side of that dispute.
It notes a shortage of data that limits research on a particular question, then describes how one team of researchers worked around it.
items.explanation: The text first notes a problem: estimating sea-level rise “requires long-term measurements, but such records are scarce in the Southern Hemisphere.” It then describes how Hunter and colleagues “addressed this shortage by turning to an unusual historical source,” comparing Lempriere’s tide measurements from 1841 and 1842, referenced to a benchmark carved into rock, with modern observations. The text therefore notes a shortage of data and then describes how a team of researchers worked around it.

A.recipe: wholly wrong template: invented comparison and confirmation
A.why_wrong: The text says long records are scarce in the Southern Hemisphere, not that sea level has risen faster there, and it compares no regions.

B.recipe: first move partly right, second move reversed
B.why_wrong: The researchers used Lempriere’s measurements to estimate the rise in sea level; the text never says they found the measurements unreliable.

C.recipe: wholly wrong template: a debate and one side’s evidence
C.why_wrong: The text describes no disagreement among researchers; it describes a shortage of data and a way of working around it.

sources.what: Research Data Australia, Historical observations of sea level at Port Arthur, Tasmania: Lempriere’s tide observations (1837 to at least 1842, digitised 1840 to 1842); a sea-level benchmark struck on a small cliff on the Isle of the Dead by T. J. Lempriere and Captain James Clark Ross in 1841; purpose: past sea-level rise in the Southern Hemisphere; paper Hunter, Coleman and Pugh 2003, Geophysical Research Letters 30(7)

Hunter, Coleman, Pugh 2003 abstract (EarthRef): records from 1841 to 1842 and 1999 to 2002 give a sea-level rise relative to the land of about 0.8 mm per year from 1841 to 2002; the result matters for the Southern Hemisphere, “where there is a dearth of other such data”

items.notes: Area: natural science (oceanography, climate history). Key D. Medium S7 modelled on 2.16 (problem in research, then a researcher’s approach). Key wording avoids 2.16’s key. Distractors: two wholly wrong templates (A, C) and one with the first move partly right and the second reversed (B), as in medium structure items.

items.passage:
The following text is from “The Serving Girl,” a poem by Gladys May Casely Hayford, a writer born in what is now Ghana. The poem was published in the 1927 anthology Caroling Dusk.

The calabash wherein she served my food,
Was smooth and polished as sandalwood:
Fish, as white as the foam of the sea,
Peppered, and golden fried for me.
She brought palm wine that carelessly slips
From the sleeping palm tree’s honeyed lips.
<u>But who can guess, or even surmise
The countless things she served with her eyes?</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined lines in the text as a whole?
options: It suggests that the girl offered the speaker something more than the meal she brought.
It reveals that the speaker could not tell what kinds of food the girl had prepared.
It indicates that the girl was unhappy about having to wait on the speaker.
It emphasizes how many separate dishes the girl served during the meal.
items.explanation: The first six lines list the food and drink the girl brings: fish “golden fried for me” and “palm wine.” The underlined lines then turn, with “But,” to “the countless things she served with her eyes,” which no one “can guess, or even surmise.” Since these things are served with her eyes rather than in a dish, the lines suggest that the girl offered the speaker something more than the meal itself.

B.recipe: LIT: “who can guess” read as confusion about the food
B.why_wrong: The speaker names the food clearly, fish and palm wine; what cannot be guessed is what the girl served “with her eyes,” not the meal.

C.recipe: INV: an unhappy feeling the poem never gives the girl
C.why_wrong: Nothing in the poem suggests the girl is unhappy; the speaker describes her serving warmly, with no complaint from her.

D.recipe: LIT: “countless things she served” read as dishes of food
D.why_wrong: The “countless things” are served “with her eyes,” so they are not dishes; the poem mentions only fish and palm wine.

sources.what: Gladys May Casely Hayford, “The Serving Girl,” in Caroling Dusk: An Anthology of Verse by Negro Poets, ed. Countee Cullen (1927), whole poem copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #76889; her own note there says she was born at Axim on the Gold Coast in 1904

items.notes: Area: literature (poem, 1927, public domain in the US). Key A. Easy F_lit modelled on 1.23 (underlined lines of a short poem, what they convey) and 1.1. Source line follows the bank’s Caroling Dusk precedent (w3b3_15) since the poem’s first periodical publication is not confirmed. Casely Hayford appears nowhere in the bank or the official items. Distractors: B and D literalize the closing image, C invents a feeling. Options start “It” like 1.23’s.

fixes: option A “the meal she brought him” made “the meal she brought”: the poem never gives the speaker’s sex

items.passage:
The following text is from Carl Ewald’s book My Little Boy, translated from the Danish by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos in 1906. The narrator is describing his young son.

He has a habit which I love.

When we are walking together and there is anything that impresses him, he lets go my hand for a moment. <u>Then, when he has investigated the phenomenon and arrived at a result, I feel his little fist in mine again.</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows that the boy is afraid to explore anything new unless his father is beside him.
It shows how the boy returns to his father after briefly exploring something on his own.
It explains why the narrator worries whenever his son lets go of his hand on their walks.
It suggests that the boy is becoming more independent than his father would like him to be.
items.explanation: The narrator describes “a habit which I love”: when something impresses his son, the boy “lets go my hand for a moment.” The underlined sentence completes the habit: once the boy “has investigated the phenomenon and arrived at a result,” the narrator feels “his little fist in mine again.” The sentence therefore shows how the boy returns to his father after briefly exploring something on his own.

A.recipe: REV: the boy explores on his own
A.why_wrong: The boy lets go of his father’s hand to investigate whatever impresses him, so he is not afraid to explore without his father beside him.

C.recipe: REV: the narrator loves the habit
C.why_wrong: The narrator calls this “a habit which I love”; he does not say he worries when his son lets go.

D.recipe: INV: a parental worry about independence the text never states
D.why_wrong: The boy lets go only “for a moment” and then takes his father’s hand again, and the narrator expresses no wish that the boy were less independent.

sources.what: Carl Ewald, My Little Boy, translated from the Danish by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos (Scribner’s, copyright 1906), section I; text copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #35543 (the Danish original’s year is not confirmed, so the source line gives only the translation’s)

items.notes: Area: literature (book of sketches, translated, 1906). Key B. Easy F_lit modelled on 1.20 (Erdrich: a sentence offering a detail that shows a trait) and 1.1. Ewald appears nowhere in the bank or the official items. Distractors: A and C reversals, D an invented worry.

items.passage:
The following text is from Helene Johnson’s poem “What Do I Care for Morning,” published in the 1927 anthology Caroling Dusk.

What do I care for morning,
For a shivering aspen tree,
For sun flowers and sumac
Opening greedily?
What do I care for morning,
For the glare of the rising sun,
For a sparrow’s noisy prating,
For another day begun?
Give me the beauty of evening,
The cool consummation of night,
And the moon like a love-sick lady,
Listless and wan and white.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe the changes the speaker notices as morning gradually turns into night
To explain why the speaker has trouble sleeping through the night
To express the speaker’s preference for evening over morning
To celebrate the beauty of the plants and birds that appear at dawn
items.explanation: The speaker twice asks, “What do I care for morning,” dismissing its “glare” and “noisy prating.” The speaker then asks instead for “the beauty of evening” and “the cool consummation of night.” The text therefore expresses the speaker’s preference for evening over morning.

A.recipe: INV: a gradual change over a day the poem never traces
A.why_wrong: The poem sets morning and evening against each other; it never describes the hours in which one turns into the other.

B.recipe: INV: a problem with sleep the poem never mentions
B.why_wrong: Nothing in the poem refers to the speaker’s sleep; the speaker simply prefers evening and night to morning.

D.recipe: REV: the morning scenes are dismissed, not praised
D.why_wrong: The speaker mentions plants and a sparrow only to ask “What do I care for morning”; the beauty the speaker wants is that of evening.

sources.what: Helene Johnson, “What Do I Care for Morning,” in Caroling Dusk (1927), lines 1 to 12 of 28, copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #76889

items.notes: Area: literature (poem, 1927, public domain in the US). Key C, the shortest option, as easy purpose keys often are. Lines 1 to 12 end at the first full stop after the turn to evening. Johnson appears nowhere in the bank or the official items. Distractors: A and B INV, D REV.

fixes: explanation and D’s why_wrong say “the speaker” instead of “she”: the poem never gives the speaker’s sex

items.passage: In 1944, Brazilian artist and activist Abdias do Nascimento founded the Teatro Experimental do Negro (Black Experimental Theater) in Rio de Janeiro. Nascimento had resolved to establish a Black theater company to combat racism after attending a production in Peru in which a white actor wore makeup to portray a Black character. The company’s inaugural production, presented in 1945, was Eugene O’Neill’s play The Emperor Jones. The company later assembled the performers for Orfeu da Conceição, a play subsequently adapted into the internationally acclaimed film Black Orpheus.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why the Teatro Experimental do Negro chose to perform plays by American writers
To compare the theater of Brazil with the theater of Peru during the 1940s
To argue that Black Orpheus is the most important work connected with Nascimento
To describe the origins and some achievements of a Brazilian theater company
items.explanation: The text explains how and why Nascimento founded the Teatro Experimental do Negro “to combat racism,” then names two of its achievements: its “inaugural production,” The Emperor Jones, and the performers it assembled for Orfeu da Conceição, which became the film Black Orpheus. The text therefore describes the origins and some achievements of a Brazilian theater company.

A.recipe: BROAD plus INV: one play by O’Neill turned into a policy and a motive
A.why_wrong: The text mentions only one play by an American writer and gives no reason for choosing it.

B.recipe: INV: a comparison the text never makes
B.why_wrong: Peru appears only as the place where Nascimento saw one production; the text does not compare the theater of the two countries.

C.recipe: STANCE plus BROAD: an argument about ranking
C.why_wrong: The text simply notes that the company assembled the performers for the play that became Black Orpheus; it never ranks that work above others.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Abdias do Nascimento: in Lima, Peru, he saw The Emperor Jones performed by a white actor in blackface and decided to create a Black theater in Brazil to fight racism; founded the Teatro Experimental do Negro (TEN) in 1944 in Rio de Janeiro; TEN premiered on May 8, 1945, with O’Neill’s The Emperor Jones; TEN organized the cast for Orfeu da Conceição, later adapted into the film Black Orpheus

items.notes: Area: humanities (theater, Afro-Brazilian history). Key D, the shortest option. Easy P_profile modelled on 1.4, 1.6 and 1.10. Details the source does not state (literacy classes, the Quilombo newspaper, the cast of the 1945 production) are left out. Distractors: A BROAD plus INV, B INV (compare is never keyed), C STANCE.

fixes: checked neighbor, kept: live text_structure_and_purpose.P_profile.easy.w3b3_19 (Victoria Santa Cruz, Cumanana, Peru’s first Black theater company) is a person profile in another country with different facts; not a clone

items.passage: Ships that are no longer needed are sometimes deliberately sunk to create artificial reefs, providing fish and other marine organisms with a durable surface for shelter and feeding. <u>One example is the decommissioned aircraft carrier USS Oriskany, which was sunk in the Gulf of Mexico in 2006, approximately 24 miles off the coast of Pensacola, Florida.</u> Before the sinking, many hazardous substances were removed from the vessel. Its flight deck now rests more than 130 feet below the surface, and the wreck has become a popular destination for recreational divers.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It explains why the US Navy stopped using the USS Oriskany as an aircraft carrier.
It provides an example of the practice described in the previous sentence.
It describes the hazardous substances that were removed from the ship before it was sunk.
It argues that the USS Oriskany is the most popular diving site in the Gulf of Mexico.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a general statement: ships “are sometimes deliberately sunk to create artificial reefs.” The underlined sentence then names “one example,” the USS Oriskany, “which was sunk in the Gulf of Mexico in 2006.” The underlined sentence thus provides an example of the practice described in the previous sentence.

A.recipe: LIT plus INV: “decommissioned” turned into an explanation
A.why_wrong: The sentence calls the ship “decommissioned” but never explains why the navy stopped using it.

C.recipe: PART: the content of the following sentence
C.why_wrong: The removal of “many hazardous substances” is mentioned in the sentence after the underlined one, and the text never says what those substances were.

D.recipe: STANCE plus INV: a ranking the text never makes
D.why_wrong: The text says only that the wreck “has become a popular destination for recreational divers”; it never compares it with other diving sites.

sources.what: Wikipedia, USS Oriskany: sunk on 17 May 2006 as an artificial reef in 210 ft of water in the Gulf of Mexico, about 24 mi south of Pensacola; environmental review and remediation removed toxic substances first; flight deck about 135 ft down (about 145 ft after Hurricane Gustav, 2008); accessible to recreational divers and rated one of the top wreck-diving sites

items.notes: Area: natural science and history (artificial reefs, a naval ship). Key B. Easy F_example modelled on 1.3 (a sentence giving one example of a general statement in the previous sentence) and 1.14. Reviewer replacement for the Promenade plantée item, a concept clone of live transitions.X1_example.easy.w1b2_17 (railway lines turned into parks, same example frame) and of the round-1 High Line item. No “largest vessel ever sunk as a reef” claim, since the SS United States is planned to take that record; no claim about fish on the wreck, which the source barely covers. Distractors: A LIT plus INV, C PART (next sentence), D STANCE.

fixes: replaced: the Promenade plantée item cloned live transitions.X1_example.easy.w1b2_17 (“cities have transformed obsolete elevated highways and railway lines into public parks”, same example frame) and named the round-1 High Line; new subject USS Oriskany sunk as an artificial reef (Wikipedia), claimed in claims.txt, key letter B kept

items.passage: In 2015, ecologist Thomas Crowther and colleagues estimated that Earth holds roughly 3 trillion trees. That number is more than seven times the previous figure of about 400 billion. <u>The earlier figure had been calculated from satellite images and estimates of forest area, without any information gathered on the ground.</u> Crowther’s team instead compiled tree counts from more than 400,000 forest plots worldwide. The researchers then combined those counts with satellite data to map how densely trees grow in each region.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It presents the main finding of the study discussed in the text.
It explains why the number of trees growing on Earth has steadily declined over the past several centuries.
It describes a shortcoming of an earlier estimate of the number of trees on Earth.
It summarizes a criticism that other researchers made of Crowther’s methods.
items.explanation: The text reports Crowther and colleagues’ estimate of “roughly 3 trillion trees,” far more than “the previous figure of about 400 billion.” The underlined sentence explains that the earlier figure was calculated “without any information gathered on the ground,” and the next sentences show how Crowther’s team avoided that problem by using “tree counts from more than 400,000 forest plots.” The underlined sentence therefore describes a shortcoming of an earlier estimate.

A.recipe: REL: the main finding is in the previous sentence
A.why_wrong: The study’s main finding, about 3 trillion trees, appears in the first sentence; the underlined sentence concerns how the earlier figure was calculated.

B.recipe: INV: a decline the text never mentions
B.why_wrong: The text compares two estimates of how many trees exist; it says nothing about the number of trees changing over time.

D.recipe: SWAP: the limitation moved from the old estimate to Crowther’s study
D.why_wrong: The underlined sentence describes a weakness of the earlier figure, not a criticism of Crowther’s methods, which the last sentence presents as an improvement.

sources.what: Yale School of the Environment news (2015): the previous estimate of just over 400 billion trees was generated using satellite imagery and estimates of forest area but did not incorporate any information from the ground; the new study used data from more than 400,000 forest plots, from national forest inventories and peer-reviewed studies, combined with satellite imagery; more than 3 trillion trees, about seven and a half times previous estimates
Crowther et al. 2015, Nature 525: 201-205, Mapping tree density at a global scale: about 3.04 trillion trees, an order of magnitude higher than the previous estimate

items.notes: Area: natural science (forest ecology). Key C. Easy F_limit modelled on 1.16. To avoid 1.16’s skeleton (two competing views, “However, many ... relied on incomplete data sets,” then a large new data set and agreement), the passage opens with the new result, then the old figure’s limitation, then the new method; no competing views, no signal word. Distractors: A REL (previous sentence’s job), B INV, D SWAP.

items.passage: <u>Until 2017, the earliest chemical evidence of grape wine in the Near East came from Hajji Firuz Tepe, a village site in Iran’s Zagros Mountains dating to about 5400–5000 BCE.</u> That year, Patrick McGovern and colleagues reported wine residues absorbed into pottery from two Neolithic settlements in Georgia, in the South Caucasus. The vessels had been manufactured around 6000–5800 BCE. These enormous jars, among the earliest pottery produced in the region, probably served as containers for fermenting, aging, and serving wine.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It identifies the older record that the discovery described in the following sentence went on to surpass.
It explains how researchers were able to detect traces of wine in ancient pottery.
It describes an earlier discovery that the researchers working in Georgia later demonstrated had been dated incorrectly.
It presents the main conclusion that the rest of the text supports with several examples.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence says that, “until 2017,” the earliest chemical evidence of grape wine in the Near East came from Hajji Firuz Tepe, dating to “about 5400–5000 BCE.” The next sentences report wine residues in Georgian pottery “manufactured around 6000–5800 BCE,” which is older. The underlined sentence therefore identifies the earlier record that the Georgian discovery surpassed, helping show why that discovery matters.

B.recipe: INV: a method the text never describes
B.why_wrong: The text says wine residues were found “absorbed into pottery” but never explains how they were detected, and the underlined sentence concerns an earlier find.

C.recipe: REV plus INV: an older record treated as a dating error
C.why_wrong: The Georgian finds are older than the Iranian ones, but the text never says the Iranian evidence was misdated; it was simply the earliest known until 2017.

D.recipe: REL: wrong role (main claim with examples)
D.why_wrong: The underlined sentence gives background about an earlier find; the rest of the text describes one new discovery, not several examples supporting a conclusion.
